claims.claim: 800 requests a second of simple indexed reads is well within what a few Spring Boot pods can handle
claims.measured: Single-row Postgres read on 1 CPU: java-spring-vt 12,731 req/s, java-spring 7,668 req/s
claims.why: A single 1-CPU container handled about 10–16 times the 800 req/s target, so a few pods have plenty of headroom.

claims.claim: Java and Spring Boot will meet the target (800 req/s, p99 under 150 ms) easily
claims.measured: Single-row query: 12,731 req/s with p99 12.39 ms (java-spring: 7,668 req/s, p99 77.87 ms)
claims.why: At saturation on 1 CPU, both Spring variants exceed 800 req/s with p99 under 150 ms, and the virtual-thread variant has a wide margin.

claims.claim: Your p99 will depend on Postgres, the network and connection pool waits, not on the language
claims.why: The tests ran each server at saturation, where p99 did differ by stack (java-spring 77.87 ms vs go-gin 6.00 ms); latency at a light 800 req/s load was not measured.

claims.claim: With virtual threads you get high concurrency from straightforward blocking code
claims.measured: Single-row DB: 12,731 req/s, p99 12.39 ms vs 7,668 req/s, p99 77.87 ms without virtual threads; 10 ms I/O wait at 256 connections: 14,571 req/s
claims.why: Virtual threads raised database throughput by about 1.7 times and cut p99 by about 6 times, and the server held 256 concurrent waiting connections at a rate close to other stacks.

claims.claim: Memory per pod for Go is ~50–150 MB
claims.measured: Peak 7–16 MB across all tests; idle 2 MB
claims.why: Even the low end of the claim (50 MB) is about 3 times the highest measured Go peak, and the claim is more than 10 times the measured figures at the top of its range.

claims.claim: Memory per pod for tuned Spring Boot is ~300–700 MB
claims.why: Under load, the claimed range is within a factor of 2 of the measured peaks.

claims.claim: Across 3–4 pods per data centre, the memory difference between Go and Spring is a few GB of RAM
claims.measured: Per-pod peak difference about 200–490 MB (Spring 209–500 MB vs Go 7–16 MB); over 6–8 pods that is about 1.2–3.9 GB
claims.why: Multiplying the measured per-pod gap by 6–8 pods gives roughly 1–4 GB, which matches 'a few GB'.

claims.claim: Go startup time is under 1 s
claims.why: Measured start-up is well under the 1 s bound.

claims.claim: Spring Boot (tuned) startup time is ~3–10 s
claims.why: Measured start-up of about 6 s falls inside the claimed range.

claims.claim: Container image size: Go is small, Spring Boot is larger
claims.why: The direction is right: Spring images are about 3 times larger.

claims.claim: Raw request speed of Go and Spring Boot is similar
claims.measured: Plaintext: go-gin 53,941 vs java-spring 13,653 / java-spring-vt 20,006 req/s; JSON: 46,183 vs 27,264 / 22,146; single-row DB: 22,138 vs 7,668 / 12,731
claims.why: In raw request handling, Go measured about 2.7–4 times faster on plaintext and up to 2.9 times faster on the database test, so 'similar' understates the gap.

claims.claim: Spring AOT or class data sharing (CDS) cut startup time
claims.why: No AOT or CDS variant was benchmarked.

claims.claim: Quarkus or Micronaut use less memory and start faster
GraalVM native image narrows the memory and startup gap with Go
Virtual threads give you the same benefit as Spring WebFlux at this load
claims.why: WebFlux was not benchmarked, so there is nothing to compare against.
